subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ACTION TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT RESULTING FROM CLOSURE OF LABRADOR LINERBOARD MILL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The announced closure of Labrador Linerboard Mill in Stephenville, Newfoundland will have disastrous and far reaching economic and social effects on the province. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie):
That this House orders that the federal government direct initiatives through every related department-DREE, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Manpower and Immigration, DND, MOT, and the Treasury Board-to examine and act through every avenue to relieve the depressed state that will result, with the objective of the rehabilitation of a potentially viable industry and to find alternatives commensurate with the area's infrastructure.

speechtext:
I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 concerning the announcement by the government of Newfoundland. Considering that the closure of Labrador Linerboard Mill in Stephenville will mean immediately an increase of unemployment by some 2,100 in the province of Newfoundland, increasing the official rate of unemployment in the province as a whole from 18.5 per cent to 19.5 per cent and if the hidden unemployed in Newfoundland are included, increasing the real level of unemployment in the province from 31.3 per cent to 32.3 per cent, a disastrous level of unemployment in that province, I move,
seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the government bring forward at the earliest possible moment a special employment program for Newfoundland which recognizes it has the worst unemployment situation in Canada and needs immediate assistance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, I will direct my question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who apparently is in charge of the increasing unemployment levels in Canada. It pertains to the announcement of the shutdown of the Labrador Linerboard Company in Stephen-ville, Newfoundland which will increase the official level of unemployment in that province from 18.1 per cent to 19.5 per cent and, if you include the hidden unemployment, increases the real level of unemployment from 31.3 per cent to 32.3 per cent. Does the minister recognize that there is a real crisis in unemployment in the province of Newfoundland which now has the highest level of unemployment in the country in recorded history, far exceeding the national average for the dirty thirties in Canada? If he does recognize it, what does the government plan to do about it?

It is not just the closing of the Linerboard factory. We have been aware of the problem in that province for some time. Through the LIP program and the Canada Works program, of the gross amount paid out across the country, Newfoundland ranked number four in money paid to a particular province. We have heavily weighted Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs to do that which we can under the job creation program. Our regional director for Newfoundland is meeting this weekend with officials of the company; I understand that the hon. Mr. Rousseau is also attending. In addition, we are looking into the possibility of an emergency response under the Canada Works program. Also, I understand there is a firm in Western Canada which might be able to employ some of the skilled workers involved. So we are on top of the situation within the programs and the funds available to us in a particularly difficult time.

Having the respect I have for private members of the House and their closeness to their constituencies and to public opinion, and as this matter is a most serious one and ought not to be left to the decision of two men, the Prime Minister of Canada and the premier of Quebec, who in the past have been very close, I ask that several days be set aside in the House to enable private members from all parts of the country to express their views on this question.
These members represent their constituencies and would be able clearly to state exactly the feelings of their constituents and their provinces. Restricting the time to 15 minutes for each member who participates would thereby secure a consensus in the House of Commons which would be responsible in every way. In consequence of the serious situation which prevails-other matters are unimportant compared to this- will the minister do his part to make possible the provision of a week in the House of Commons to enable private members, who otherwise will have no opportunity to speak, to express themselves clearly to the government of the province of Quebec and to its people?

subsubtopic: NATIONAL GUIDELINE REQUIREMENTS OF SPACE IN PUBLIC BUILDINGS AND VEHICLES
speechtext:
Does the government have national guidelines which control the amount of space required in public buildings and vehicles as related to number of persons allowed in such buildings or vehicles at any one time, to ensure safety and to restrict overcrowding and, if so, do the guidelines include (a) size of seat space (b) distance between seats (c) width of aisles (d) number of exits and, if so, what are the details?
Order Paper Questions

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: NATIONAL GUIDELINE REQUIREMENTS OF SPACE IN PUBLIC BUILDINGS AND VEHICLES
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, the amount of space required in public buildings to ensure safety and to restrict overcrowding is controlled by the requirements specified in the National Building Code of Canada, (a) No; the requirements do not specify the size of seat space with fixed seats, this being left to good design based on box office experience, (b) Yes; the minimum distance between rows is 16 inches, with no more than 7 seats between any seats and the nearest aisle except for "continental" type seating where up to 100 seats are permitted per row provided there is a door to a means of egress provided for every three rows of seats, (c) Yes; the minimum width of aisles is 30 inches for 60 seats or fewer, 36 inches when seats on one side only are served and 44 inches for all other arrangements. The width is required to be increased one and one half inches for each five feet in length towards an exit, (d) Yes; usually minimum of two but number and size dependent upon building construction, building fire protection, building occupancy and occupant load.
In so far as Transport Canada is concerned: Yes, there are such standards for aircraft used in public transportation. The maximum number of passengers is determined by airworthiness regulations and specified in the Aircraft Type Approval. The size of seat and distance between seats is not regulated. The width of the aisles and number of exits are regulated and vary with the passenger capacity of the aircraft. The details of these standards are contained in numerous airworthiness regulations.

Improvement Loans

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
First I shall deal with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, Mr. Speaker. As hon. members know, for the most part our fishermen make up an important segment of this country's small business community. On April 21 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) issued a press release pointing out that additional funds would be available for loans to fishermen under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. I have read the press release and wonder how the fisheries improvement loans legislation is to help the fisheries of Canada, especially our inland commercial fishermen. The Inland Commercial Fishermen's Association represents its members in the Northwest Territories, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and parts of northwestern Ontario.
I hold in my hand a document listing loans made under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. This document really is part of the April 21 press release put out by the Minister of Finance. Looking at this list, I see that British Columbia, in 1976, received 241 loans for a total of $5,578,877. On the other hand, Alberta received one loan totalling $2,550. I point out that the fishermen of Alberta are represented by the Inland Commercial Fisheries Association. Alberta fishermen must sell their fish to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. Glancing down the list, I see that Saskatchewan, in 1976, received one loan of $3,500. I would point out that Saskatchewan fishermen, as well, sell their fish to the FFMC.
I note that according to the list, in 1975 Manitoba fishermen received six loans under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act for a total of $19,816. I point out that Manitoba produces 57 per cent of all fish caught by the inland commercial fishermen of Canada, but Manitoba fishermen received a measly six loans in 1975 for a total of $19,816. Looking at the figures for Ontario, I note that the picture improves somewhat. Ontario fishermen, in 1975, made 12 applications for loans, for a total of $200,800. Casting my eye down the list, I note that the greatest amount of money made available by way of loans has been directed to eastern Canada. Apparently our commercial fishermen in the prairie provinces have not in an overwhelming way enjoyed the benefits of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act: it has not been widely used in those provinces.
I was appalled to learn on April 20, the day before the Minister of Finance issued his press release, that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) intended to launch a $41 million program to rebuild the fisheries of Canada. The program apparently is not to be a rescue operation: it is designed to rebuild our fishery. Unfortunately, the press release of April 20 makes no mention of activities in central Canada involving the Inland Commercial Fishermen's Association. Mr. Speaker, those fishermen are in just as desperate straits as the fishermen on the east and the west coasts of Canada. They depend greatly on federal government help. Many of them run small fishing operations and must sell their fish to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. That corporation runs what I call a processing "palace" in Manitoba. Do you know that it cost more than $5 million to build that processing "palace" for the FFMC? I suggest that the govern-

ment bungled in building such a large plant, since one half the size, or even two-thirds as large, would have been big enough to process all the fish supplied by the inland fishery of Canada.
One sees large loans being directed to our east and west coast fisheries, but not to our inland fisheries which are most important. I suggest that our inland fishery is as good as any in the world, if not better, for our freshwater species of fish find their way not only to the tables of Canadians but to export markets. At least two-thirds of the inland freshwater fish caught are exported to the United States, and even to France. Even so, our freshwater fishermen face the same sort of dilemma confronting fishermen on the east and the west coasts. They cannot meet the high cost of operation. They, too, would like to benefit from the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. However, as I have mentioned, in Manitoba there were only six applications approved, for a total of $19,000. That would not buy even one boat for a fisherman.
The Inland Commercial Fishermen's Association covers the Northwest Territories, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Northwestern Ontario. At a recent meeting of the Northern Manitoba Commercial Fishermen's Association they said they were going to put forth a very strong resolution to the conference dealing with the restructuring of FFMC by removing political appointees from the board, the board itself to be made up of 51 per cent of fishermen and/or their representatives. The remaining 49 per cent should be made up of provincial appointees from Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. Ottawa should also be allowed their representatives. The chairman would be elected to the board from the provinces. Our fishermen can see the dilemma they are in. We are getting fewer and fewer fish. Ten years ago the Inland Fishermen's Association of Canada were producing 70 million pounds of fish. Today it has dropped to 35 million pounds. The reason is that fishermen had to get out of the business; they did not have the finances with which to continue. A loan of $10,000 would be of great benefit to these small commercial operations. This is what we have to look at, because those individuals who no longer fish make up part of the one million unemployed in Canada.
Having a piece of legislation like this brought into the House, without the minister being here, is a disgrace. This is not only important with regard to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act but the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Small Businesses Loans Act.
The Northern Manitoba Commercial Fishermen's Association has proposed an economic development program to encourage the building of primary processing plants throughout the north. The Fisheries Improvement Loans Act can play a very important part in helping these fishermen by having a processing plant in the north adjacent to the lakes being fished commercially. Much of the fish taken out of the nets today is thrown into the bush because there is no market for it or it is too far to transport it to the processing plant in Transcona. I believe fishermen should be paid for every pound of fish they
April 29, 1977

remove from their nets. Enabling these fishermen to make applications for loans under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act would not only help the industry but it would help to relieve the unemployment problem in this country.
The fishermen could have their product processed and packaged in the north as well as any by-products that are saleable in the consumer market. For example, it could be used for such things as pet foods, fertilizer, calf meal, and so on. These Fishermen are doing their best to remain employed. However, with inflation and the high cost of operation, many of them find it easier to go on unemployment insurance or welfare than to carry on with the fishery.
I am pleased to note that under this amendment the maximum amount that can be loaned at any one time is increased to $75,000. However, when I look at the $41 million program to rebuild the fishery in western and eastern Canada, as well as the $130 million that has already been poured into that industry, I find it rather odd that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment cannot bring himself to assist inland commercial fishermen. As I mentioned before, they are just as important as fishermen in other parts of Canada, and they are becoming unemployed in the same way.
Getting back to the question of locating primary plants in the north to accommodate the local area, packing sheds have to be built. Although there is provincial assistance at the present time, it does not assist all fishermen. It assists fishermen up to a maximum of $1,000 if they produce a certain poundage of fish. They receive ten cents a pound for transportation on the first 10,000 pounds picked up from the lake. Of course, many fishermen produce in excess of 10,000 pounds. They really are not helped that much.
I wish to comment on a remark made last night with regard to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. The fisherman either has to go to a small bank in an isolated community or to a bank in a far away community, because many northern communities do not have banks. Because he may not be known to the local banker, I believe the federal government should take on the responsibility of approving the loans. Not one loan was made, under this act, in the Northwest Territories. I do not imagine any banker there would know the situation and would consider making a loan to a fisherman in the Northwest Territories. That seems to hold true for the prairie provinces as well.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) toured western Canada a week ago he said that he was standing on his record. If he were standing on the record of loans made under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, I am sure he would feel the pebbles through the soles of his shoes. It is certainly of no assistance as far as the fishermen are concerned and, therefore, it is not a program to boast about.
In conclusion, the Inland Commercial Fishermen's Association is going to be a strong voice. They want a better price for their product. They want to be able to produce natural resources. The fishery of inland Canada is a renewable resource. If properly looked after, harvested properly, and if good conservation methods are used, it will serve us forever.
Improvement Loans
However, if the fisherman cannot make a half decent living and is not able to meet his commitments, a loan under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act for up to ten years may help him over the slump until he can again be productive.
As I mentioned before, there are presently 6,000 members of the Inland Commercial Fishermen's Association. However, if something is not done to assist the fishermen, the membership will drop to between 2,000 and 2,500. The balance of those fishermen will be unemployed, because there is no other work in that area. They will either go on unemployment insurance or welfare. As a result of the government not recognizing the high unemployment level in the north, the prairie provinces have again been throttled.
We are now in a 13-week to 14-week waiting period. Many fishermen who fish for only a limited time each season will not qualify for UIC payments, so they will just have to go on welfare. Many of the people I am talking about are treaty Indians who are the responsibility of the federal government. Giving a loan under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act might enable them to carry on. The fishermen are selfemployed. These are small operators, not large corporations. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the small businessman is the real backbone of Canada, yet the government is not making it very easy for small business. The minister does not seem to be interested. I say this because I do not see him in the House today.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the passage of this legislation unduly. This really is a minor bill. It makes small changes in terms of increasing the amount which can be lent, and extends the basis for qualification. To this extent it is a minor attempt to help small business.
If the government was really interested in doing something for small business, instead of bringing this tired old act back every year and asking us to approve a couple of amendments to the figures, it might be entitled to some credit. But the bill before us is no credit whatsoever to the government. It does nothing except try to match inflation with the amount which can be lent and with the capital value of eligible firms.
Let me give an example of what could have been done. One of the steps would be to fix a percentage of the funds which banks are obliged to lend. This is a government which is supposed to know something about business. I do not think any of the ministers who sit opposite has ever gone to a bank to try to get one of these loans. It is clear that if a bank is not obliged to lend money under this legislation, it will choose not to do so. Instead, it will make loans on which it can charge a higher rate of interest. So they do not channel customers into the use of the funds available under the bill. The minimum it should have is a mandatory percentage allocation requirement.
Another thing about this whole loan procedure is that if you are from a small town and you go into the bank and ask for a loan, you find that the local banker has authority to go up to a

April 29, 1977
Improvement Loans
minor amount, say $10,000. If you want $20,000, $30,000 or $40,000, you have to go to the head office in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Montreal or Toronto. The bankers in the head offices have lunch, not with small businessmen but with people who have massive capital needs and massive capital investments. So you will find that the small businessman who defaults on the tiny loan which the local manager did not have authority to make and had to trot off, like some toady, to the head office to get approval, is going to be chased until he pays it. Ele will be hassled and harassed. The same day, in the financial pages of the papers, you will find a firm which has gone into default with the Bank of Montreal for $5 million. What happened to those people, and what happened to the bank in terms of its balance-sheet at the end of the year? It is the small businessman who is harassed because he doesn't have clout with the bank. If the government wanted to do something, it would present a bill which would give the small businessman some clout with the bankers. Until they start doing that, they are not interested in small business at all.
To me, one of the classic cases of injustice in small business affected a couple of fellows trying to get a business going-I do not think they would mind if I mentioned the name- Quadra Athletics. The only way in which they can make their business grow is by being allowed to buy sporting equipment outside the country. They gross about $500,000 a year. They are willing to pay any tariff the government wants to place on this sporting equipment, but the only way they can survive is by picking up special sporting equipment manufactured abroad. The law as it is now requires possession of a quota before these goods can be imported, even if the firm is prepared to pay the duty. The same stuff is carried at Hudson's Bay, at Woolworth and other major stores. These poor fellows cannot even bring in stuff and pay the tariff in order to compete with these large companies. This quota system, allegedly to protect the textile industry in Quebec, is driving good, small businessmen right to the wall in the most unfair way I can imagine.
Here are two businessmen who realize there is a problem in the textile industry in the east and are willing to pay duty to protect workers in textile mills in Quebec. That is fine. But for goodness sake do not tell them that they cannot bring the products in so as to compete with businesses which already have a quota. That is the destruction of the whole free enterprise ethic. People in this House are continuously reminding us of the extent to which they support the free enterprise ethic. Let them examine that piece of legislation in terms of any sense of fairness to the small businessman.
There is some kind of hardship provision which is a meaningless clause in terms of the whole question of import duties. Put yourself in the position of a young man who has invested every dollar he has ever had, who has faith in the free enterprise system, who goes out to make a buck and finds that the government tells him, "You are out of business. You've had it. You cannot bring the product you wish to sell into the country." It is a horrendous bureaucratic nightmare and it is a

matter to which the government should give serious consideration.
I want to tell hon. members a story about gas stations in the area I come from. I used to have some experience of small lease-owned gas stations. The lease contract is a story in itself. Arthur Hailey should really write another book about the relationship of a small operator of a gas station with a major oil company; it is a slavery contract. But I point out that the provincial government and the federal government have to deal with a major problem in the gasoline industry and its use of self-serve facilities to drive the small businessman right out of business.
When self-serve came to my riding the cost was running about 4 cents a gallon less than that of the fully serviced gas station. As a result, customers were conditioned to use selfserve stations again and again. Then when customers had been conditioned the price rose dramatically. In fact, right now in my constituency I can go to the corner of 6th Avenue and 8th Street and buy gas at 81.9 cents a gallon. If I go to the self-serve, the price is 82.9 cents a gallon. Where is the fairness and justice in that? The oil companies operating these self-service stations have succeeded in driving the price of gas even above that charged by the fully serviced gas stations.
Here is a small businessman who needed protection, the small guy who spent his whole life working in his station, thinking he had something, working an 18-hour day. What does he wind up with? He winds up with an unemployment insurance cheque, if he is lucky. I do not intend to throw blame around on a party basis; however, this is the kind of protection we have failed to give small businessmen. The small businessman has been driven right to the wall because we have not examined the impact which the major oil companies have on the market and how the pricing of their products relates to the small businessman in the retail gas industry.
It is disgraceful that I can now go to a full service station and that poor entrepreneur has got to charge me less than the guy across the street in self-serve, but still provide services like wiping the windshield, looking at the oil and checking the tires. I get nothing from the self-serve but gas. Because we have been conditioned to use it, we do not care any longer. They have got the volume of traffic and they have destroyed the small entrepreneur, the small businessman who worked so long and hard to develop something.
The oil companies do not allow for goodwill; there is no such thing as far as they are concerned. They are the only ones who have any goodwill in a small gas station, and what does the poor guy who has faith in what he calls the competitive system get out of it? He gets nothing out of it and this after a lifetime of work. Not only can he not sell goodwill; now he has nothing to sell because the self-serve station is driving him out of business anyway. No one in this country has lifted a finger to do anything about it. That is a group that needs a lobby in parliament. All of us get lobbied around here by I do not know
April 29, 1977

how many groups, and it is about time some groups that are not represented had a chance.
I know that the Federation of Independent Businessmen tries, but they have a heck of a job in terms of the wide variety of small business problems. We have let a person who is not working for wages but who is working many times at the cost of his health trying to build up a business go to the wall, out of sheer neglect. This really is a tragedy in this country.
Something else we should examine is the rate of bankruptcies in small business. In the province of British Columbia-it is also probably true on a national basis-such bankruptcies are at an all-time high. We had better ask ourselves, and certainly this government had better ask itself, why they are at an all-time high. The reason they are at an all-time high is that we have been trying to tell the House, budget after budget after budget: If you take away the purchasing power of ordinary people and do not reduce taxes at the middle and lower levels, you take away the capacity of people to buy from the small businessman.
The butcher, the baker, the candlestick-maker, the guy who is trying to make a living as a small businessman, is not helped by $1.2 billion worth of corporate tax concessions. They do not go to him; they go to the majors, to the companies which dominate the economy. This little piece of fluff is all we are producing for small businessmen in this place, yet we give $1,200 million to the major corporations. Where are this government's priorities? They are certainly nothing to do with small businessmen.
We are accused of being anti-business, but this party is the one party in the House which has been pro small business. We really want to see people given an opportunity to have purchasing power so they can go to the small businessman and buy his products. But all we have had is legislation making it easier for major corporations to drive the little guy right to the wall and out of business. Take policies as an example. You can buy jeans at the Bay for one price, but if you are a small retail clothier you have to pay a different price. Someone should look into what happens there in terms of the competitive market and the kickback deals that go on.
There is a whole range of irritants so far as small business is concerned. For example, one is interest rates, which this bill could have done more about. There is our failure to be serious about monopolies. I suppose this is free enterprise rhetoric, but I do not think anyone here believes it any more. The fellow, in this system, who is really being hosed and who does not have a lobby to look after him is the small businessman. He cannot compete with the majors. He has been driven to the wall by the corporate giants, and has a labour union pushing him on the other side. I am not going to stand here and say that it is not the duty of a labour union to organize. I think it is. But give some attention to the guy being squeezed both ways. I have not seen a single piece of legislation in this House since 1972, that has done a thing for him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada

speechtext:
How about when the unions squeeze the small businessman?
Improvement Loans

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext: I just said that. My friend from Vancouver East (Mr. Lee) asks about unions squeezing small business. He is perfectly right. Small business has a terrible job on its hands meeting union demands. Because of their lack of competitiveness, and because of the way we have allowed the major giants to dominate the market and the economy, the small businessman is driven to the wall in terms of union demands. But that is not an argument against unions; that is an argument against this government for its failure to do something for the small businessman so that he has the capacity to pay union rates, proper rates, for people who are only asking for a decent wage in this society. I think everybody needs to be in a trade union in Canada. We would be a lot better off and it would rationalize the system. It is not a case of whether the small businessman is organized or not; it is a case of his simply not having enough revenue to pay the people in his firm, and the firm goes under. The reason the firm will go under is that there is not a single thing in this government's budget to look after small business. There is a continuing attitude that if we help Imperial Oil, somehow small business will be helped. The reverse is true.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in this debate because I happen to represent a constituency which has an interest in all three phases of this bill. I have constituents who would be interested in a fisheries improvement loan if one were available. I have farmers who are always big spenders and who have an interest in a farm improvement loan. I also have, as most other members, many many small businesses in my constituency.
It saddens me to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) delegate the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand) to pilot through this chamber a bill which, it would appear, is of little consequence to the Minister of Finance. It further saddens me that the minister delegated to pilot through this bill is not taking an interest in a bill of such significance.
During the last few minutes I have listened to two speakers with similar problems to mine. The first was the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) who represents a riding with a large number of fishermen in northern areas. His riding adjoins mine; he is on the Manitoba side of the border and I am on the Saskatchewan side. We have parallel problems. He has high rates of unemployment in his area, and I could make the same speech in terms of my own constituency. He made my speech for me; therefore I will not repeat a lot of the points he made. I jotted down some notes and intended to cover many of the subjects he mentioned. The problems he referred to in the fishery in his area are the same as mine. I suggest that for the minister even to bother introducing these amendments to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act is a travesty.
The hon. member for Churchill has already mentioned one lonely loan to the province of Saskatchewan for fisheries improvement-and we have to spend our time amending it so we can carry it forward for another three years. I ask: What for? There is no need for this type of legislation, because it is

April 29, 1977
Improvement Loans
not fulfilling the requirement. You will note that I did not say there was no requirement for cash and I did not say there was no need for money in the area.
To come forth with this type of legislation and to parade it before fishermen indicates to me that neither the Minister of Finance nor the Minister of State for Small Business took the time to even consult with the fishermen. It saddens me because many fishermen in northern Saskatchewan are Indians. Many of these fishermen are receiving unemployment insurance. Many of the people in northern areas are crying out for manpower assistance under the Canada Works program.
The government have had ample opportunity to do something. I have to come to the conclusion that they do not even know what it is all about and, worse still, they do not care. Anybody who cared at all and wanted to improve the situation would have taken the time to set up a meeting at any place in northern Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba-you name it- and say to the meeting, "What are your requirements?" The first thing they would tell the minister is that no banker in the area will give them a loan. This is what the hon. member for Churchill said. And that is what my Indians are telling me: They say, "How can we even approach a bank?" There are no opportunities; there are no institutions there. There was an opportunity to come forward with something which would provide loans for these people. The Minister of State for Small Business could have come forward and said they were establishing for the first time institutions in northern areas staffed with people who knew the requirements and trusted the fishermen.
The first thing a banker does is develop trust for his customer. The way he develops that trust is by giving him a small loan and seeing how he does with it. I know; I have tried to get money from bankers from the time I was 18, when 1 first started farming. After 25 years I had to quit my bank because they were trying to see how much they could peel off me. After 25 years this was the way they treated me. What do you think they are going to do with a new customer? The one business that the banks are in is to make money. Get that clear. They are not there for your good. If it helps you, you are the one who has to manage it. If you are the one who gets the loan, you have to make sure you pay off that loan. On top of everything else, they want a government guarantee in order to even consider you for a loan.
To continue to deal with the requirements of the fishermen, anybody knows that their requirements are far greater in northern areas which are remote from the business areas of the southern parts of Canada. Their transportation costs are higher and their gasoline costs are higher. In some cases they have to fly in fuel at $2 a gallon. We talk about $1 a gallon. How would you like to pay $2 a gallon? Talk about inflation!
They also have the requirements of nets and boats. If the government had wanted to attempt to solve this problem, here was an opportunity. They could have steered away from just a standard stereotype loan. We should have ample experience. At the rate of one a year we are not going to get very much experience, are we? That one loan tells me one thing. It tells

me that the requirements of the local fishermen are not being met. The banks could not care less, because they would have to grant the loan at a lower rate of interest. They are not about to rush into that field. Why should they? As in my case, as in everybody's case, if the banks have you in a position where they can squeeze 13 per cent out of you, they will. They are not going to look around for a 9 per cent interest loan, regardless of any government. That is incidental. It is a laugh as far as the banks are concerned. I tell you that from personal experience.
Many people have said, "Why are you still in the farming business?" I keep telling them that I am in the farming business for two reasons. One is that politics is so uncertain. The second reason is that in politics nobody has to tell me about the situation because I know first-hand what the story is. I would like to relate some of my experience. I am sure everyone else could relate a similar experience. The government has not done its homework. It has not set up requirements for the fishermen. After we pass this bill, for three more years you might as well not have brought it in. Three years or 15 years later it will make no difference.
Last year I had delegations of fishermen who were crying to know how they would be provided funds for the ice harvest. Unless we provided some assistance they were going to go on unemployment insurance or welfare. A lot of people in the northern areas are on welfare. Surely there has to be some cash input.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at one o'clock I was commenting on one aspect of this bill, that is, the operation of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. As the House is well aware, I represent a Saskatchewan riding. The minute one mentions Saskatchewan to anyone, he assumes that naturally you come from the prairies. It might surprise the House that of some 700 fishermen in Saskatchewan, there are about 350 commercial fishermen in my riding. In the past I have spoken of their needs and concerns, and I find it disgusting to have to rise in my place and make the comments I am making now. The Minister of State for Small Business has had ample time to do something about the cash requirements of fishermen in all areas. In fact, if I were him I would have refused to have anything to do with that aspect of the bill. He has had ample time to introduce amendments and to study the requirements of the fishermen in that regard. This he did not do. As a result, after royal assent is given to this bill the situation will not change one bit.
April 29, 1977

People involved in commercial fishing are far removed from national banking institutions. They cannot possibly establish any credit. Who fulfills this requirement? Institutions such as Hudson's Bay, co-operatives and other enterprises. What is the result? People are committed to these businesses, not because they want to but because they have to finance their operations. This is an area where the government could and should step in. The government could go in directly, as has been mentioned by the hon. member for Churchill, or it could pass other legislation in this House. I dare say nobody would oppose an attempt to introduce legislation to compel the banks to issue at least a certain number of loans to certain industries in which there is a definite need. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) suggested that there should be a certain percentage, and I agree with that. The way it is now, banks simply disregard this legislation. We have no power over the banks. We stand as helpless children before the banks, pretending we are doing something for these people. This legislation has been on the books since 1944. We have had ample opportunity to consider the requirements, but we are not doing anything.
Two suggestions have been made today, and I would like to make another one. I suggest that the banks should be obligated to submit to the government reports of all the applications which have been made under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Small Businesses Loans Act, giving the reasons they were turned down. At least then the banks would not have control over the economy of our country as they have today. If the banks did not have any money, I would say there would be no point in compelling them, but I have been a member here almost 20 years and I have seen banks in small communities start off with small, cubby-hole businesses where there was perhaps a manager, an accountant and a teller. However, now these institutions operate out of beautiful buildings with glass fronts which are air-conditioned and modern. Now there may be a dozen people working in some of the banks in some of the smallest places. In addition, other banks have moved in because there is a requirement for them.
I have already said that banks are not in the business of doing anything but making money. I am glad to see the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) here this afternoon. We have the power to do something with regard to banking. We have the authority to introduce legislation. I am sure as good corporate citizens of this country the banks would comply. All we are asking is that people be helped to get out of the mess they are in. Perhaps I have dealt with this matter at some length, but fisheries improvement and farm improvement and small business improvement loans require that type of attention.
Because of the limited time I have, I will move to another area-small businesses. All hon. members have small businesses in their constituencies. I find it strange that in 1976 the number of loans made in Saskatchewan was down 50 per cent from 1975. Why suddenly should there be such a dramatic change? It is not that there is no requirement there. The banks
Improvement Loans
just felt that they were not going to provide loans under this legislation, and nobody had any power over them. People have come to me asking what I could do. All I could do was write to the Minister of Finance, who indicated he could not compel the banks to do anything.
1 am sure hon. members opposite parade across the country saying, "Look at what we have done for small businesses. We have introduced amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act and to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act". The government has done nothing. It has done nothing but make it possible for some newspaper writer who might like to list all these "accomplishments". Anyone who is not involved might think that the government has an impressive record, when in actual fact nothing has happened. The need is now even greater.
I am sure all businessmen borrow every year, but their credit is limited. We should be able to introduce an amendment which could provide short-term, 30-day loans, and if they cannot be paid in that time perhaps a different rate could apply. That might encourage small businessmen to control their financial arrangements. However, we are not doing anything. Banks across the country are Financing their big buildings. Granted, perhaps big buildings are needed to improve working conditions, and so on, but in addition banks are still showing tremendous profits. They have taken care of themselves very nicely. However, I always thought these institutions should be here to meet our requirements. If they are not, perhaps we as legislators have a responsibility to make them serve us, instead of themselves.
There were 241 businesses in Saskatchewan which benefited from the Small Businesses Loans Act, but there are many small businesses in the communities of Saskatchewan. There are nearly that many small businesses in even the smallest communities. The fact that only 241 businesses in Saskatchewan benefited under this legislation means that the legislation is not meeting the need. Businesses which are not covered under this legislation have to pay interest at the prime rate plus. General Motors, of course, can get a good rate. General Motors is a good risk. But the small businessman, who is the mainstay of the economy of this country, can not. Let us start thinking about the small businesses of this country instead of big corporations like General Motors. General Motors can look after itself. In all the years I have been in politics I have not been concerned about big corporations that have earned plenty of money. I am not concerned about the large corporations; they can look after themselves. But I am greatly concerned about our small farmers, our struggling businessmen and the little people of this country. I have devoted my time to looking after their interests.
If we are to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Small Businesses Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, let us do a proper job; let us do what is necessary to fulfil the needs of our farmers, fishermen and small businessmen. I suppose newspapermen, people in the gallery and

April 29, 1977
Improvement Loans
ordinary citizens think that $75,000 is a great deal of money. I point out to such people that a tractor today costs about $55,000, and a combine about the same figure. Also, you need much more than a tractor and combine for running a farm. Mr. Speaker, the increase to $75,000 in the limit does not even compensate for inflation. The cost of farm machinery has risen very steeply in the past few years, and if you tell the Farm Credit Corporation that you possess total assets of $75,000, they will tell you that your operation is not viable and you are not eligible for a loan. To city people, $75,000 represents the price of a home. But you cannot start a farm with that kind of capital. You need a lot more money than that.
The question arises, do farm improvement loans mean taking an undue risk when money is lent to a farmer who may have fallen on hard times? I say that you cannot compare the risk of lending to a farmer with the risk of lending to a young man who wants a loan for a car. You cannot compel the banks to lend money, but if a farmer has not done well for a few years, that is no reason for thinking him a bad risk. After all, the farmer has money invested in his farm: he does not want to lose it.
I told Your Honour something of my personal experience. I dealt with one bank for 25 years, as I said, then I discovered I was older than I realized, and now I must say that I dealt with that bank for about 30 years. I once went to that bank when the loan limit was $15,000, they granted me a loan. I could not get a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation as a member, but I could obtain one under the Farm Improvement Loans Act from the bank. Because I had already taken the limit I was forced to take a loan at the bank's current rate of interest. After all, I had to make a living; I had to keep up with the economy. Of course, the bank lent me money at the prime rate, plus 2 per cent. On top of that I was required to pay interest every month.
The bank introduced a cute little twist into this transaction, of which farmers wishing to borrow money may be unaware. Although the interest rate per annum was a nominal 12 per cent, because I had to pay interest by the month it meant that the bank's return was much greater than that. It took the money I paid as interest and lent it out again. Clearly, it obtained a far greater return than 12 per cent. If I paid an interest instalment in January and my loan had until December to run, it meant that the bank could use the money I paid in January for 11 months, and so on. Probably the bank was earning close to 15 per cent on the money it lent me. But they told me I would get the money at 12 per cent.
Not many people stop to think what the bank is doing under this cute little arrangement. After I had dealt with that bank for 25 or 30 years, I discovered one day that the bank manager would not grant me a loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. At that time the loan limit had been raised to $50,000 and I could have qualified. Of course, the bank manager had me over a barrel, because I had previously taken out a loan and had given some titles as security. In the end he said to me, "Well, we will give you the loan, but under such and such terms." By that time I had had enough and refused

the bank manager's offer. I shopped around for a loan. I tried all the banks in my area and in that way rearranged all my business.
I am saying this for the record because I want all farmers to do the same. Shop around for your money. Forget about your friendly bank manager. He is only your friend as long as he is making money from you. As soon as he stops making money, watch out. Then you will see if he is your friend. So I say, shop around for your money. Every housewife does it when she shops for groceries, so why should a farmer not do it when he shops around for money, which is like any other commodity. It makes good sense to shop around, and especially good sense to shop around for money. The bank manager may pretend to be your friend, but you will discover how friendly he is if you neglect to make an interest or a principal payment.
We could compel the banks to lend a certain amount of money at a certain rate. Never mind simply increasing loan limits under the legislation and then telling everyone, "Look at what we are doing". I say the government is not doing anything for the farmer, because anyone who knows anything about farming knows that $75,000 will not go far these days. You cannot even start a farm operation with that amount of money.
I want to know why farmers' applications for loans are turned down. What reasons are given? Many farmers who have been refused loans have come to me and asked, "What can I do?" I asked one farmer if he was within the limit. He replied that he was. He said that his banker was cutting down the amount of money he would lend under the farm improvement loans legislation. One need not be a genius to know why this is happening. If a farmer is desperate, he will pay the bank 12 per cent, or whatever rate it is asking, because the farmer knows that the cost of machinery will rise in two months and he cannot afford to pass up a good deal today. That shows the bind we are in. But if the bank had to report to the Minister of Finance and say why it turned down the farmer's application for a loan, the story might be different.
I do not say that every applicant should be granted a loan, but I do say that the banks should report their reasons for not granting a loan. I realize that they have to run their own businesses. If we allow the banks not to grant loans under the legislation because they can make more money if they lend at ordinary bank rates, I say we are not doing our job. How are we to improve the economy if the banks hold farmers in their hands and turn down their loan applications? Personally, I have to think twice before I agree to pay 12 per cent. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the attitude of the banks will not help to get our economy going again. They like to make large loans to single customers. The bank manager plays a little golf with his client, sips a cocktail and asks the client to sign on the dotted line. That operation is easy. It takes considerably more trouble to provide a service to our little fishermen and farmers, some of whom may live 200 miles from the nearest bank.
Credit unions have proliferated across this country because the banks have not filled the need. I remember hearing of one man who said he would raise his own finances without going to
April 29, 1977

the banks. When someone asked him where he would apply, he said he would approach the credit union because credit unions are to be found almost anywhere these days. Clearly, the banks have not met our people's needs in remote areas. They have been falling down in this regard. They are private institutions. The government is not a private institution. It, too, has a responsibility and it has not been meeting the need of farmers, businessmen, and fishermen. That is the saddest part of all this.
At the same time I say that I will have to be in favour of this legislation. How can I not be in favour of increasing the amount? The government has me over a barrel. That is the magic of government manipulation. If I vote "no", it appears as though I am against increasing the amount from $50,000 to $75,000. If I vote "yes", it appears as though I agree with the legislation. However, it does not fulfil the requirements of the fishermen, farmers and small businessmen of my constituency. With this kind of legislation the government is not doing anything about the unemployment problem.
I think I have said enough to indicate that this legislation is futile. Some people ask why we are frustrated. This legislation is an example of the frustration we suffer. Members opposite can laugh, but we want to do something. This legislation is no credit to the Liberals. They say that the PC members only make speeches because it is their duty to be in opposition. That is not what I want to do around here. The Liberals had better open their eyes and see what is happening in this country, rather than glorying in what is happening to another party. It is what is happening in this country that concerns us. Before bringing forward another amendment like this it should be the requirement of the minister responsible to see whether it is what is really required in this country. He can then bring it in and ask that we devote one day to it.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) wanted a few days to deal with another problem. There are other problems in this country. This place is like the RCMP with their list of the ten most wanted men. The minute they find one, there is another to take his place on the list. We as legislators are also dealing with the ten most important problems. The minute we resolve one, there is another to take its place. They are all important. Rather than becoming preoccupied with one problem, we should be concerned with all segments of this country. Instead of spending all our time listening to television reports and reading newspaper articles which are preoccupied with only one subject, let us look at all the requirements and ensure that what we are doing is for the good of the whole country.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
Members opposite have been asking that ministers get into the field, as just suggested by the hon. member for Mackenzie, in order to find out what the people want. This is what the minister has been doing since his appointment. He has been getting as much as possible from the people in the front lines, the owners and operators of small firms who have borne much of the brunt of the economic problems besetting western nations in the past few years. It is the small entrepreneur who has been squeezed from both ends, with higher costs for raw materials and skilled labour but with no chance to pass on these increases without risking being priced out of the market. The small businessman has had a tougher time than big business or big labour.
The federal government's anti-inflation program has begun to take hold. We have brought inflation down from the doubledigit horrors of a year ago. Investment and production are up again and we have begun a moderate recovery. But these are still not fat days for the small businessman. This is why the post of Minister of State for Small Business was created. The role of the portfolio, as I see it, is not to bring out a bag of magic tricks to solve some old and thorny problems. Granted, there are some things that can be done without undue delay, such as tackling the paperwork burden imposed by government on the small firm. But I think that it is the feeling of small business in Canada that what is needed is less government, not more.
Therefore, I know the minister wants to become a focal point for the concerns of small business as they relate to the federal government. He wants to play the role of the voice of small business in cabinet. But most of all, right now he wants to be a good listener. He wants to hear from organizations like the Retail Merchants Association of Canada. He wants to know what small businessmen want from government. I

April 29, 1977
Improvement Loans
applaud him in his stated intention of not attempting to establish yet another bureaucratic empire in Ottawa.
The Speech from the Throne last fall described small business as the backbone of the economy. Coming, as I do, from an area with many small enterprises, where the old-time, frontier-style spirit of individual enterprise is still very much alive, I can appreciate the truth of that statement. We British Columbians are not that far removed from the frontier days. Only three generations ago much of the land there was bush. We know that the spirit of the small entrepreneur, the man or woman with a small stake and a dream, is still a driving force behind not only our economy but our whole society here in the west.
Almost two-thirds of Canada's work force, some five million people, derive their livelihood from working in the more than
250,000	small Canadian firms. Many of those firms are the result of one man's or one woman's will to succeed in the face of a thousand obstacles. Too often it seems that the federal government is one of those obstacles. The small entrepreneur feels that he has to spend too much of his time filling in census forms from government or worrying about the paperwork for taxation, pensions, unemployment insurance and workmen's compensation. On top of all this, the small businessman has to do the government's work for it by collecting both federal and provincial sales tax.
At the same time as government is pressing the small businessman too close, it is too remote from many of his real needs. He cannot find out first-hand about government contracts, grant and loan assistance and technical advice. This feeling persists despite an effort to decentralize services through some 85 branches of the federal business development bank, as well as regional offices of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Supply and Services.
In British Columbia there are now 19 branches of the Federal Business Development Bank, four more than last year. One of them is in my riding. The FBDB is providing assistance to small operators in B.C. to the tune of $460 million-to some 3,600 small firms in this province. However, the FBDB is only one of the many initiatives and programs of the federal government aimed at helping small business. The anti-inflation program has helped many small firms to deal with labour costs which otherwise might have put them in a difficult position. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) drew attention to this earlier.
Of more direct benefit have been incentives such as the two-year fast write-off for manufacturing equipment and the reduction in the corporate tax rate for manufacturing or processing firms which has been in effect since 1972. Then there are incentives such as the reduced corporate tax rate for companies controlled by Canadians which can be eligible for a reduced rate of 25 per cent on the first $150,000 of taxable income. The opposition conveniently forgets these things.

The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce administers some 15 programs to improve the efficiency and competitiveness of Canadian industry. Some provide grants for research and development, industrial design, productivity studies and export marketing. Others guarantee private sector loans to restructure industry in order to take advantage of export opportunities or to adjust to import competition. The federal government also provides grants and loan guarantees to establish, modernize or expand manufacturing and processing plants, as well as commercial or service facilities.
I think this line-up of initiatives demonstrates clearly that the federal government has had a long-standing commitment to the interest of the small businessman. Of that there should be no doubt. The concern which has arisen and which has led to the creation of the post of Minister of State for Small Business is that the incentives and programs of the federal government must meet the real problems. That is the job of the Minister of State for Small Business. Businessmen and government officials alike are concerned that these programs provide the most appropriate assistance and that they be available in the areas where they are most needed.
Clearly, there is a need for better communication between the small entrepreneur and the government. Clearly, the government must assume the responsibility for improving that communication. This is why I was gratified to see it reported in the Financial Post the other day that the Minister of State for Small Business was embarking on a program to improve communication between business and government as part of what is called "enterprise development".
As many hon. members have pointed out, this replaces what have been called the "alphabet soup" programs, so named because of their numerous acronyms. For example, some of the programs with which businessmen have had to deal include the Program for the Advancement of Industrial Technology (PAIT); the Industrial Design Assistance Program (IDAP); the Program to Advance Productivity (PAP); the General Adjustment Assistance Program (GAAP); the Pharmaceutical Industry Development Assistance program (PIDA), and so on. Hon. members will note the plethora of programs which small business has to deal with. Herein lies the gap between small business and government. This is why the government has embarked upon this new course at the initiative of the Minister of State. It is a worth while program and I look forward to seeing what other developments come out of it. It is my understanding that both a national board and regional boards are to be created and that those who will sit on these boards will come from business and industry.
I might say that every time I meet with my chambers of commerce or individual business constituents and listen to their problems they tell me that finance is what most concerns small businessmen. This being so, a competitive interest rate would seem best to suit the needs of the small business operator. I believe the amendments to the Bank Act which will shortly be forthcoming will go a long way toward improving the financial climate for small business. I know the government wishes to work closely with the private banks because
April 29, 1977

they have always been an important part of the small business community. But I think we can make the Federal Business Development Bank more effective. Since it began operations last year, the banks has certainly shown a capacity for creativity in its approach to the small businessmen, and it is quite possible for the Federal Business Development Bank to become the one-stop contact for small business with the federal government.
I know that when my constituents come from British Columbia to Ottawa to deal with federal officials, they often Find there are four or five agencies with which they have to meet, involving running from meeting to meeting all over town just to complete a simple piece of business. I have heard quite a number of these horror stories, enough to know that this is no way to run an outfit. If we can cut through the interdepartmental wrangling-and I trust the minister will be successful in finding ways of doing this-we can improve the climate for the small businessman and, hopefully, provide him with one-stop service without unnecessary red tape.
The assistance programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce are currently being re-evaluated to see how they could be made more accessible to the small operator. Most of this assistance has previously gone to fairly large firms, but I think programs like the industrial innovation and adjustment incentives program could be made to benefit smaller companies. Decentralizing the administration of these programs would also make them more accessible to small businessmen.
Mr. Speaker, I have outlined what I consider to be a few good places to start in improving the lot of small business in Canada. I have no doubt there are many others, and I will seek them out. An important part of the government's consultations will be with the provinces. Provincial governments, too, are concerned for small businessmen and have programs to assist them. The federal government should work with them to avoid duplication.
I know that many of my constituents own or operate small businesses. Many of them built those businesses from the ground up, putting in their savings, their sweat and their hopes. They could have earned a safer and easier return on investment by putting their money into a savings account. But they did not. TThey chose to invest in Canada the hard way because they had faith in our system and in their own abilities. I respect that faith. I respect their hard work. I respect a man or woman who stands on his or her own feet and tries to create something where there had been nothing before. That kind of spirit is vital to our society and I want to see it flourish and prosper.
The government can help. Sometimes it can help by just bowing out of the picture. Sometimes it can help by providing the right kind of aid in the right way. There is room for improvement in the effectiveness of government services to the small businessman, especially to those operating outside the larger cities. There must be more decentralization. There must be more export opportunities provided to the small entre-
Improvement Loans
preneur. There must be more information available about big projects where the subcontractor can get in on the action.
I want the government to provide small business with the help it really needs and wants. I want small business in my area, through consultation, to let me know what its needs are. I want the government to become a useful partner to the gutsy men and women out there who are making Canada a place of opportunity. But most of all, I want to protect and help foster the spirit of the individual entrepreneur, because that spirit is one of the greatest contributions a Canadian can make to his country.

Mr. Speaker, the Chair certainly decides what is a point of order, but as a member certainly I can express an opinion on what is a point of order, and it is my opinion that that is not a point of order. It is up to the Chair to decide, but we can have an opinion.

The minister in charge of small business should go down to St. John's West and get out on the Cape shore and around Placentia Bay and see where small business needs to be helped, instead of bringing in penny-ante bills like this raising loans from $50,000 to $75,000. Let him get out to areas where some good could be done if a few dollars were spent on public works which are badly needed. It is going to raise the loans that the minister can guarantee under the Farm Improvement Loans Act from $1,400 million to $1,550 million. Not bad, not bad! What is it going to do under the Small Businesses Loans Act? It is going to raise the figures under the Farm Improvement Loans Act from $350 million to $600 million. Well, it is going to raise the loans from $70 million to $80 million-ten million measly dollars is what they are going to increase the loans for fisheries. That shows how the Government of Canada views the fisheries-a $10 million increase for fisheries; a $250 million increase for small business; and a $150 million increase in the loan limits for farmers. I am surprised at fisheries getting even a $10 million increase.
When we look at the fisheries what do we find? The program started in December, 1955. You are going to be amazed, Mr. Speaker, if you have not recently researched this point yourself, to see what has been loaned since 1955 under this program, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. Mr. Speaker, you are not going to believe it. From the inception of the program in 1955 to March 31, 1976, 8,101 loans amounting to $59.5 million were made. The bailiff and the sheriff are not harassing the fishermen if they miss their payments for a year because of bad weather, illness, a poor catch or a catch failure. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE LOANS TO $75,000 FOR IMPROVEMENT OF FARMS, BUSINESSES OR FISHERIES
speechtext:
There will not be any need for fishermen if they do not have fish. We are hoping that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment is going to be very careful in the quotas he comes up with for 1978. Canada now controls the 200-mile limit. If Newfoundland is to have any say at all, fisheries have got to be a large part of it. The Minister of Fisheries and the Environment controls the 200-mile limit. This year, for the first time, Canada is setting its own quotas.
Is the minister going to be timid, frightened, and afraid of the Russians, the Poles, the East Germans, and the French who fish out there? I suppose one bark from the French and the minister will run ten miles; and one yap from the Russians and he will disappear altogether. Is he going to do what is needed for Newfoundland and Canadian fishermen? Is he going to establish tight quotas this year? Is he going to take his time before he establishes them? Is he going to consult with the people who are interested in the issue-the fishermen and the skippers of trawlers who fish out there?
I spoke to a trawler fisherman in Trepassey several months ago, and he told me that never once had a federal fisheries minister or a federal fisheries officer asked him for his opinion on quotas; how they could be enforced; what the problems were; or what should be done with net sizes, surveillance or whatever. To his knowledge, he did not know of one trawler skipper who had been consulted by the federal government on this question.
The quotas should not be set too soon. There should be consultations with the government of Newfoundland; there should be consultations with fishermen's unions; and there should be consultations with the fish merchants and the people at Memorial University who are doing research in this area, such as Stratford Canning of the Centre for the Development of Community Initiatives, so that we will have proper quotas that will take into account the inshore fishermen.
Inshore fishermen are really small businessmen, small entrepreneurs, and they should be consulted. Their interests must be protected by the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment when he sets quotas for this year, not as in past years when he paid them no attention because from Ottawa inshore fishermen look inefficient. They do not appear to be as efficient as large trawler fishermen. Inshore fishermen appear to be outdated and outmoded by people who forget an inshore fisherman lives in an ideal setting and environment where he owns his own home, can grow some of his own vegetables, does not have to pay rent or mortgage, is out in the fresh air, cuts his own firewood, etc. But they think he is inefficient because his boat cannot move beyond two, three or ten miles from the shore.
Let me assure the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment that we do not want that way of life changed in Newfoundland and we do not want our fishermen moving into urban slums. We want them left where they are, and means provided for them to make a decent living, all of which can be done if the 200 mile limit is administered properly.
April 29, 1977

For example, the Centre for the Development of Community Initiatives at Memorial University has done a lot of work on what should be done by the minister in setting quotas. ICNAF has set quotas for 1977; the minister sets them for 1978. Fie has a heavy responsibility and he must remember our inshore fishermen when he sets the quotas, particularly with respect to Hamilton Banks where too large an amount has been given to foreign fishing vessels to take this year. The minister should consult with Mr. Canning and his researchers before he sets the quotas. If he does not, we will make the welkin ring in 1977 and in 1978, as I promised the fishermen in St. John's when they elected me. I said to them, "When you elect me to go to Ottawa, I will not be quiet. I will present your interests. What we have to do is make the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) more afraid of us than of the Russians, the Poles, the East Germans and the French. That is the only way you will ever get proper quotas set in the 200 mile limit." We give due notice to the Minister of Fisheries on that subject.
1 have another example of the government's confusion, not mentioning its cynicism. It is an example of its casual abandonment of any principle of proper conduct when it comes to national unity. I will deal with that on another occasion.
Now I want to deal with one hand not knowing what the other hand is doing. Here is a bill to help the small businessman. I received a letter today which will show you how concerned the government is about small businessmen in the city of St. John's. The city manager, Mr. E. P. Henley, supports the position taken by Mr. Innes, chairman of the Port of St. John's Authority. By the way, he was a Liberal candidate in St. John's West last year. He is a very fine gentleman but he was not elected, and naturally I am glad of that. He is a public minded citizen. I suppose it is not too strange to have a Liberal put in that job. In any event he was right about pilotage rates in St. John's when he wrote to the Minister of Transport on March 28. The Atlantic Pilotage Authority, who are controlled by the Department of Transport, will now raise their pilotage rates in St. John's harbour for vessels under 25 units, by 60 per cent to 126 per cent.
When you talk about the Anti-Inflation Board, 1 do not know what applies to small business. How does this affect small business? That thought comes to my mind. I will tell you how, Mr. Speaker, because it is small businessmen who serve these vessels which come to St. John's harbour. Last year there were 1,279 vessels in St. John's, 662 were Canadian and did not require pilots, and 617 were foreign vessels of which 444 were foreign flag trawlers. There are small businessmen called ship chandlers and others who supply those vessels with provisions, look after their needs, and act as agents for them. They contribute considerably to business in the port of St. John's.
Most of these trawlers are small vessels under 45 units, and now the Atlantic Pilotage Authority wants to raise their pilotage rates by 60 per cent to 126 per cent. What kind of stupidity is this? This will drive these foreign trawlers out of the port of St. John's down to the ports of Saint Pierre and
Improvement Loans
Miquelon where they will be treated properly and hospitably, to the detriment of the business in the port of St. John's. They may go to other ports in the Atlantic region, if we are lucky, but more likely they will go to Saint Pierre and Miquelon. They will not want to go the rest of the distance.
There are Spanish vessels which travel and work in pairs- Spanish pair trawlers. In the past they required only one pilot when they came to port. The pilot is in the lead vessel and the second vessel follows the first one into port. Now they will have to have two pilots, and with the increase of pilotage charges for small vessels, the increase will be from $400 to $905.10 because of this piece of arrant stupidity which will drive these foreign vessels out of our ports down to Saint Pierre and ruin the small businessmen who service them, damage the St. John's dockyard which employs 350 people- all because of the parsimonious and skimpy attitude of the CNR in not getting all the work it should these days-and endanger the future of all these people because these trawlers will not be coming in for repairs.
How can the government claim it is trying to help small businesses when, on the one hand it will help them get larger loans from $50,000 to $75,000, and on the other hand it allows some bureaucrats or some swollen elephantine pilot of the pilotage authority to try to make a vicious grab by increasing from 60 per cent to 126 per cent pilotage fees on small vessels in one year? We will not put up with it. We will not tolerate it, and I am sure hon. members of the House will back me on it. I know we are only a small province and we come here unprotected, not even protected by the game laws, but we appeal to the fairness and spirit of generosity of the Canadian people to help us and protect us from these bureaucratic excesses. Of course our great protector, when he takes office next year, will do that. I am referring to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
I appeal to the Minister of Transport to see that this pilotage outrage is reversed. I will ask him nicely first, but the next time I speak in the House on this issue, if this is not changed, I will change my tone. I will not be half as friendly.
Now I should like to refer to farming for a moment. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) made a brilliant speech. It is easy to see why that hon. member is elected time after time in Saskatchewan, and I prophesy he will be here as long as he can draw a breath and blow a whistle.

There is a gap in this program. There is something wrong.
Farmers in Newfoundland are not as wealthy as farmers elsewhere. Why are they not receiving the benefits of this program? I challenge the Minister of Agriculture to forget about the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and pay attention to the farmers of the country. He should forget his childish peeves about the publicity the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is getting. He should come to Newfoundland and take care of the farmers there. I will help him find them. He should ask them why this program is such a failure as far as they are concerned.
I do not have the correct figure, but I would venture to guess that out of the $3,362 billion in loans made since 1945, Newfoundland farmers did not get as much as $1 million out of the whole thing. Any Minister of Agriculture doing his job

would have gone to Newfoundland as soon as those figures became known at the end of 1975-76 and found out what was the trouble.
