To be more serious, what this country needs is more entrepreneurship, more individual enterprise. That is one of the things we are lacking in Newfoundland. There are not enough people with managerial expertise. There are not enough people who are willing to take a risk. Why is that? Because whenever anybody is ready to do that, the Liberal government appeals to him to hand out something to help the party over the next election. That is a large part of the reason. We need money spent on management training and accounting training. We need some agencies which will help people who have a few dollars, who are willing to take a risk but who need more money. This government has never made that available.
We have the Newfoundland Labrador Development Corporation in Newfoundland, but that is not enough. It is partly financed by the federal government and partly financed by the province of Newfoundland. It is able to put money into equity. It can invest in equity, and it can make loans, yet its record is not very successful. Governments in Newfoundland for 25 years made the great mistake of trying to create an industrial paradise, if there is such a thing. You cannot create large, heavy industry in a place like Newfoundland where geography and economics dictate against it.

There are other, smaller opportunities, but for those to be seized people have to have access to some training in order to get some skills, and they also need money. They should take a risk and use some of their own money, but this program by itself is not sufficient.
I do not think that $1.5 million is a large enough limit for small business. My idea of a small business is a business which is far larger than a business which has a revenue of only $1.5 million a year. For example, the dockyard at St. John's, Newfoundland, is to me a small business. It employs 350 people. It was owned by the government of Newfoundland, but it is now owned by the Government of Canada under the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada. It was given by the Government of Canada to the CNR to run for the government. CNR has run it since 1949. I do not remember exactly-because I do not have the figures here-what its annual revenue is, but it is certainly in excess of $1.5 million. The future of that enterprise is by no means secure. The 350 jobs provided by that enterprise are important to St. John's West and Newfoundland, and they cannot be lost. This operation could be more efficient if the Canadian government or some other agency were willing to help finance an expansion of its repair facilities. The operation needs a syncrolift.
The dock at St. John's West is old fashioned. It was built in the 1920's by the Newfoundland government when Newfoundland had nothing. The government had almost no credit. All it had was faith in the future. A dock was built in St. John's. There is a dry dock there, and once certain vessels go on to that dock to be repaired, no other vessels can join until all the work is finished on the original vessel. Therefore the drydock often has to turn ships away. The graving dock has been flooded, and it will be another two or three weeks before any other vessels can be taken on. What is needed is a syncrolift, a piece of equipment which will take vessels out of the water and up on to the proper space on the dock where they can be repaired and discharged again while other vessels are in the graving dock.
The expenditure required is not huge. The amount is only $5.5 million. That investment is needed to put that facility there. I am now corresponding with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Transport, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) about this to see if we can get the money. How can we do that when ministers treat us with disdain, arrogance, and disinterest when we ask questions about how they are going to solve some of the problems in the free enterprise system. How can we show that we are sincere when we heap one tax after another on citizens' shoulders at a time when they are trying to overcome the problems they face because of the present economic downturn in the nation.
We have to try to wake up the government. I do not know how to do that without dropping a time-bomb on its members and waking them up in that way. Even if it did go off, I do not know whether they would hear it. That is the sad situation that faces opposition members.
The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski) made an excellent speech today pointing out the problems faced by the farmer. He stated that $75,000 for farm improvements is not a big deal when it costs close to that to buy a new tractor or combine.

The town of Truro has been one of the healthiest economic communities not just in Nova Scotia but probably the whole country. Now it faces an unemployment rate of somewhere around 20 per cent. With that degree of erosion in the economic climate of the nation, we will probably have one and a half million people unemployed before this year is over. The town of Truro has a spectrum of small business concerns which have always produced a buoyancy in the community. When everywhere else was in difficulty, the town of Truro remained healthy. However deep a recession may have been, there was still a buoyancy in the economy of that small town, indicating that we would get out of the recession. It helped us over the humps and into a period of employment and prosperity. I hope we will not get into a situation where it will take another world war to resolve the problem. With the kind of warfare there would be these days, there would be no one left to worry about unemployment insurance, jobs or anything else. This country has almost reached the point where that is the only kind of stimulation that would bring us out of the very deep recession into which we are moving.
When we do get legislation before the House that could produce a good debate with good ideas to point out the weaknesses and pick up the economy, the government members could not care less. They do not seem to care whether the legislation is good, bad or indifferent. They do not even put up any defence of the legislation. It is shocking that no one on the government side even gets up to argue the points that we make. They just do not care. The only time they get excited is when we point out that the ministers involved in the legislation are not present in the House. They get sensitive, upset, and worked up when we mention that fact.
If parliament, and in particular, the government, is to have any respect for the business community it must, surely, show respect to the business community. Instead, we get silence from the government front benches, a disinterest which almost reaches the point of being obscene. No constructive suggestions have been forthcoming with regard to what the government may be offering.
I do not know where we are going. I say to the government that its attitude cannot continue. The legislation before us affects three segments of our economy which are vital to the nation's prosperity. As long as we allow our farmers to remain in difficulty, as long as we allow our fishermen to be incapable of meeting the challenges of the day, not only internationally but internally, as long as we say to the small businessmen who are producing most of the taxes we need for everything that we, in effect, could not care less about them, the mess in which this country finds itself will continue. Surely it can take some of this paper and produce whatever label it wants to put on cans of swordfish so that the fishermen of Nova Scotia can go back to work.
There are 101 things the government could do for small businessmen, farmers and fishermen. This particular piece of legislation is like a drop of water in the ocean. It will not even make a ripple. I say to the government it had better wake up to the fact that unless it is sympathetic to the small businessman's point of view there is no way in which we shall overcome the tremendous problems associated with the depression in which the country finds itself at the present time. The sooner the government wakes up to this fact, the better off Canadians will be.

speechtext:
that Bill C-231, respecting trafficking in exotic pets, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have introduced this bill again this session because it seeks to deal with a problem which arises in this country and one which, I think, is prevalent throughout western Europe and North America. I refer to the desire of an ever-rich population to engage in what I might term a kind of luxurious whim whereby individuals, at the expense of animal wildlife enjoying visual pleasures, and in some cases perhaps companionship pleasures, are subjected to an experience which I feel is simply not justifiable.
There is a very low rate of survival when animals are taken from the wild and sent through a channel of communication eventually to reach pet shops and finally the homes of rich North Americans and west Europeans, who can afford to bring these poor animals out of their natural habitat. In some cases this exercise has no effect on the survival of a particular species because enough of them are available. In other cases this is simply not the case. The trafficking in some exotic pets does have an adverse effect on their ability to survive in their natural habitat. Indeed, some are being pushed to the point of extinction by this what I will not describe as a "sick" desire, but nevertheless a desire which reflects the kind of materialistic society we have, wherein we decide we would like to have some kind of strange animal in the house and it is just a question of paying the fee. This is catering to whim on the part of the exotic pet trade and is at variance, I believe, with basic human principles of decency in the treatment of wildlife generally.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, the whole purpose of this private member's bill is to produce an interaction which I think is healthy. I have received a fair amount of criticism of
April 29, 1977

this bill, a lot of which I think is legitimate. In a democratic, open society such as ours there really is not that much justification for too much government interference in the exercise of personal whim, even though there may be fairly strong arguments against the exercise of whim. Providing there is some kind of balance, criticism is justified to a point; but how can we strike a proper balance?
I suggest that this bill is at least a starting point; it is not the final answer. It gives the government some means of control. There may be simpler ways than I have suggested, and I hope at the very least that this bill will stimulate some action on the part of the government which will institute a form of control which will not unduly interfere with the individual's right pretty well to do what he pleases in our kind of society. At the same time I hope it will eliminate or at least control excessive abuse of mother nature which is inherent in some of the practices which lead to animals finally ending up in pet shops and homes in this country.
Let me give an example of one of these nefarious practices. The killing of the mother chimpanzee or female monkey species is carried out in order to take the child, the young monkey. To me, Mr. Speaker, this is a revolting practice, one that cannot be justified by any commercial argument that may be advanced by the pet trade.
On the other hand, there are a number of pet species which are in plentiful supply, and some imported species can be bred in this country and can multiply. Once a basic breeding stock has been established, pets can be supplied to meet public demand. I see no reason why this sort of pet trade importation should be prevented, and that is not the objective I am seeking in this bill. This is one criticism I have received which I think is a legitimate one. I should like to see any legislation that this government or a future government may decide upon include control, yet have flexibility sufficient to allow the pet trade to develop a healthy breeding stock to supply the Canadian market.
I should like to refer to other criticisms I have received of this bill, because they are relevant to the debate. The word "exotic" has been criticized on the ground that it is too general a term. What is exotic to one person is not exotic to another. Zoological establishments should not, in the view of some critics, have the sole priority in the obtaining of animals. Zoos, especially private zoos, are operated for private gain, and their interest is in having animals to exhibit to the general public, rather than supplying animals for viewing by private citizens in their own homes. So there is not very much distinction between the two, except that more people have the benefit of viewing animals in a zoo than animals which are in private homes. Some say there is no distinction between a private zoo and a home with a pet, because in theory there is control, though perhaps more control is possible in a private zoo.
The bill is also being criticized on the ground that we already have in this country adequate quarantine regulations, and other countries have adequate export regulations. I agree that we have sufficient quarantine regulations but I do not feel the export limitations which exist elsewhere are adequate. As
Exotic Pets
we well realize, the price paid for many species of animal in Canada is such that the profit potential in underdeveloped countries which export these animals is so substantial that any amount of local regulations would be insufficient to prevent the illegal exportation of animals for which a demand exists. Therefore the place at which proper control can and must occur is the Canadian border.
The whole question of assuring adequate and proper transportation methods for bringing these pets into the country is something which presumably would be part and parcel of any enforcement of control by our own Canadian authorities. This is something that can be worked out. It can be worked out in the case of agricultural livestock, and it certainly should be and can be worked out in the case of these other species of animals.
There is an argument in criticism that the bill, as proposed, actually would undercut the beneficial efforts of wild livestock breeders, in some cases, to improve their breeding stock and in effect increase in the world the total number of such animals that are now threatened in their local habitats. There may be some reasonable case with respect to certain species for that particular argument. In any event, the purpose of this bill is not to have this particular wording passed. The purpose is to encourage the government to take some steps to bring in measures which will eliminate the worst things which are happening; measures which will permit a certain amount of control, and will attempt to eliminate the most nefarious practices of harvesting wildlife from their natural habitat. Part of my original intention in promoting this bill in the first place is that this will afford some protection to Canadians. In the case of some reptiles and in the case of some insects that are being imported, some health danger is inherent in their importation and there is some danger to public safety as well.
I cannot see the justification for importation for private use of an overabundance of reptiles and the kind of things that are going on, as well as some insects like tarantulae. They may be great visual items, but I hardly think that this kind of catering to whims is acceptable. There is a balance between the kind of flexibility that should be allowed in our open society and what is the public good. In this case we will have to strike a balance between the two. There is a balance that is possible.
I would urge the government, therefore, to move toward instituting some control along the lines suggested in Bill C-231 as well as those suggested in Bill C-234 proposed by a colleague of ours in the House, the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine). These two bills provide a start for a government process which it is to be hoped will result in the establishment of some form of protection for this huge flow of wildlife that is now pouring into the country from all sections of the world to cater to this materialistic society of ours that keeps seeking new novelties. I am not entirely against them having these novelties, providing it is not done in a cruel way at the expense of these species' survival in their natural habitat.

No, I was not alluding to any members. I was referring to the title of the bill which is an act respecting trafficking in exotic pets.
1 am very happy to have the occasion this afternoon to speak on Bill C-231. It also gives me the occasion to relate to the House some experiences I have had with the import of some of our so-called exotic animals.

But I realize, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-231 has several very commendable objectives. It provides restrictions designed to prevent the importation of animals that could not live in Canada or that could die in transit. It restricts the international market for animals that are often captured by cruel or illegal means.
However, this bill raises several problems. First, it duplicates existing legislation and then, I do not think it will achieve its purpose and it finally fails to set forth several other objectives. Let us go over these points one by one, Mr. Speaker.
One of the objectives is the protection of endangered species. Now Canada has signed and applies the agreement on the international trade of endangered species of wild animals and plants.
I must point out to the hon. member that the Canadian government, by signing this convention, went further than Bill C-231 because the agreement protects not only animals but also plants like orchids. In the agreement on the trade of endangered species, the latter are classified under three various categories. The first concerns species that are forbidden entry for commercial purposes in Canada, while the two others list the species which may be imported only under an export license delivered by the country involved.
I wish to underline that the agreement does not apply only to living animals that can be sold as pets but also to every animal product such as fur, bones, shells, and so on. The agreement on the international trade of endangered species is implemented by the Canadian Wild Life Service which comes under the Department of Fisheries and Environment.
On the other hand, if I am not mistaken responsibility for Bill C-231 would fall under another department, namely Industry, Trade and Commerce. So we would have two government bodies responsible for two sets of overlapping regulations that might give rise to different interpretation. This would be more than embarrassing for zoos or scientific organizations that might wish to obtain exotic animals in the public interest.

The international convention provides for the protection of endangered species and presents their harvesting in overly large numbers from their natural environment. Such a bill would therefore be more restricted in scope and less effective, only adding confusion to the situation. Another concern put forward by the hon. member in his bill involves the threat of contamination posed by the importation of living animals. Protection measures have already been initiated. All animals entering Canada must either have a certificate of good health issued by a veterinarian, or be examined by specialists from the Department of Agriculture in Canada, according to their country of origin. So once more there is no need for extra legislation to that effect.
Let us turn now, Mr. Speaker, to another goal, that of preventing mortality during transportation. Any animal can actually be moved safely, if the person in charge knows how to go about it. I know that in Canada all kinds of animals can and have been transported, even whales and whooping crane eggs. I assume that the legislation aims at preventing actions by unqualified persons, but there are already laws and regulations to prevent such practices. The Canadian government however is powerless to prevent such offences before the animal comes to Canada, before it has been moved in other words. Bill C-231 cannot guarantee that animals imported into Canada would be moved by proper transportation methods, and it is highly improbable that any Canadian act could do so.
But the last thing to do would be to prevent entry into Canada of animals being moved under inadequate conditions. Presumably they would have to be sent back to their point of origin under the same conditions, which would only compound the harm.
This brings us to the third declared object of this legislation, namely to control the importation of pets that are unable to adapt to Canadian weather or to captivity within the confines of private homes. But on what basis are we going to act? On weather conditions that prevail in Victoria or Frobisher Bay? After all, once in Canada, the pet can be brought anywhere, even in a condominium. The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that it would be virtually impossible or, for all practical purposes, difficult to translate the intent of Parliament into a series of regulations.
Besides it is perhaps a good thing that pets cannot survive on their own if ever they get away. Let us look at all the disasters which we have caused. I refer in particular to rabbits in Australia. We have here in Canada starlings which were brought in from Europe and which are now quarelling with native birds over the few possible locations for nest-building. We also have aquatic plants from Asia which are now beginning to block canals and irrigation systems in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia.
Those species imported from other continents and brought into Canadian wilderness often find themselves deprived of the natural balancing of their original environment, such as predators, diseases, pests and so forth, and can therefore threaten our plants, animals, crops, rivers and so on. Provincial wildlife organizations and the federal government have met to develop
April 29, 1977

ways and means of facing this serious threat. When they come to an agreement, perhaps they will decide that new legislation should be introduced. Any control system, however, will have to be developed so as to spell out a specific approach to solve this problem. Its purpose should not be to restrict the trade of exotic pets, but rather to deal with the more general problem of transportation, here in Canada of species which may threaten the fragile environmental balance.
In my opinion, Bill C-231 is an example of an inappropriate piece of legislation. Take for instance the case of another domestic animal which does not fall within the scope of this bill and which many wild life conservationists are greatly concerned about. I am referring to the common country dogs that irresponsible owners often leave free to roam or abandon, instead of having them destroyed when they no longer need them. Roaming dogs become wild and attack and destroy deers, a situation for which wolves are often blamed and made to suffer through intensified hunting. As a hunting and outdoor sports enthusiast, I can say that, at least in Ontario, this problem of roaming and wild dogs is a very serious one which must be dealt with. I do not think that by blaming on other forms of Canadian wildlife the damage caused to the deer stock by these wild dogs we will deal effectively with this problem.
I also think, Mr. Speaker, as I said at the beginning, that a story should be told in the House. I had the opportunity last March to attend, as a parliamentary delegate, the Water Resource Conference in Mar del Plata Argentina. I had the pleasure of meeting our ambassador in Buenos Aires who told me an interesting story. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in March 1975, the House gave the royal assent to Bill C-373, a bill making the beaver our national emblem. The bill was entitled: Bill C-373 to provide for the recognition of the beaver as a symbol of the sovereignty of the Dominion of Canada.
I would like to relate this anecdote which illustrates some of the mistakes that can be made when well intentioned but ill conceived measures are put forth. The story concerns the national symbol of Canada, the beaver. Apparently, after the war, out of great generosity on our part we sent some 20-odd pairs of beavers to Argentina. They were set free and allowed to establish themselves in southern parts of Argentina in Tierra del Fuego. Being of Canadian stock, very prolific and highly productive, they reproduced in the millions. They had no housing problem in Tierra del Fuego, they fed on good forest products, and took it upon themselves to flood the plains where sheep grazed.
This problem created such a difficulty that the Argentinians decided that our national emblem was a pest, so they put a bounty on the beavers. However, they did not know how to control them. The economic consequences of the beaver, our national emblem-I am sure the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan) will take exception to this-were such that right now in Argentina it is an unwanted species. It
Exotic Pets
was considered an exotic animal at the time it was brought into a country where it had not existed previously, but as it turned out it is now endangering not only the wood stock but also the pastures, with serious consequences to the sheep population.
The Canadian ambassador in Argentina told me that he had made arrangements to obtain some traps. Traps were delivered duly, but the people in Argentina did not know how to use them. Consequently, during the conference we made a special effort to have people from the James Bay area, who were at the conference with us, go to Tierra del Fuego. They are trappers who will show the Argentinians how to trap our national emblem.

Mr. Speaker, I related that little story because I think it indicates clearly enough that we must be careful when we import or export those exotic animals or other animals which adapt with difficulty to the new conditions of the ecosystem.
I might also add, Mr. Speaker, that irresponsible dog owners, and I want to revert to the question of dogs because I am a hunter and one who finds much pleasure in Canadian forests, I want to revert to the problem of damages caused by wandering dogs and dogs which are set free by owners uncaring about the consequences. I think that problem creates a new situation, by introducing into the environment, the ecosystem, animals which are not only dangerous, but adapt very badly to the environment. I think that man, as a source of changes, must be careful not to introduce within nature things which have disrupting effects and eventually cause us more hardships. We have glaring examples in urban areas where we see in Ottawa, for example, stray dogs and cats in the streets. I think that the problem may have been partially solved in urban areas, but out in the country and the forest we should be particularly careful not to damage the environment by such irresponsible actions.
Mr. Speaker, this leads me to the third reason why I am against the passage of the bill before us. The last provisions deal with irresponsible owners who may indirectly cause the extinction of some species which may be threatened or which have adapted to the environment. Are we to deprive serious individuals from the possibility of owning any pet because others more irresponsible cannot properly care for those animals? This is naturally a very serious matter and I do not know the answer.
I think hon. members should try to point out to their constituents the need for pet owners to assume their responsibilities in that regard. That is the only way to improve the situation. That will not be done by passing such a legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude by saying that I am sympathetic to the subject matter of the bill the hon. member put forward today, but I think the factors I have mentioned should be taken into account, particularly by paying more attention to the human side of the problem and not by trying to legislate on behaviour, for it is difficult to legislate on attitudes, and the human being has one failing: that of often

Mr. Speaker, I did not plan to speak on this bill, but once I got a good look at it, I felt I should tell the House about the experience of one of my constituents when attempting to bring exotic birds into the far northern part of Canada. This constituent is a Yugoslavian. He is a lover of birds. He has many exotic birds in captivity, and he looks after them very well. Just one year ago this month he went over to Yugoslavia to visit. While there he bought a $700 talking parrot, and he was told by an employee of Air Yugoslavia that he could bring the parrot back to Canada with no problem at all. However, the only way he could bring the parrot back was to buy a ticket for the bird. He bought a ticket and flew back on Air Yugoslavia.
When he bought the parrot he also bought six pigeons to bring back to northern Manitoba. This is a true story. It actually happened. I did not go back to my office to get my correspondence because I know the story in detail.
With his parrot on his arm and with a chain around its leg, this individual arrived at Chicago. He got out of the aircraft and walked right through customs in Chicago without a question being asked. The parrot was talking all the while. Everyone was so amused with this talking parrot that they never asked its owner if he had quarantine papers or anything else. The parrot was on this person's arm, and the pigeons were in a basket he was carrying at the same time. Not one soul asked him a question as to whether he had proper papers.
The individual spent six hours in Chicago and took a Northwest Airlines flight to Winnipeg. He had to keep his parrot and his pigeons right in the cabin with the rest of the passengers. He was not allowed to put them in the baggage hold because of the danger of suffocation. This person arrived in Winnipeg, and as he went through the Canadian customs he was stopped right there.
I became involved with this matter after the individual arrived in Winnipeg. He was waiting to get customs clearance for his parrot and the six pigeons. I contacted the Department of Agriculture, and it was pointed out to me that it was impossible to bring the birds in, so this chap went to Northwest Orient Airlines and paid for a ticket for the parrot and the six pigeons to go back to Yugoslavia.

It was quite apparent from all this literature that if the birds did not pass certain tests, they could not enter Canada. At least we cleared up that aspect of the matter.
Let me tell the House a story concerning the pet shop in Thompson, Manitoba. The story is about a chimpanzee which was brought to Canada from the United States. It arrived in Winnipeg, during the winter. The Thompson pet shop had a customer for the chimp. The owner of the pet shop managed to bring the chimpanzee as far as Winnipeg, where it arrived without any difficulty. It was held in Winnipeg for about three days while the pet shop owners tried to get it through customs. Apparently this country and the United States had not entered into a reciprocal agreement to cover animals like the chimpanzee. There was no problem getting it out of the United States; the difficulty lay in getting it into Canada.
This chimpanzee, worth about $1,500, spend three days in Winnipeg. The long and the short of it is that it contracted pneumonia, was shipped eventually to Thompson, Manitoba, and died two days after arrival. I add that the chimpanzee was not insured. I recite this story to show why I support Bill

C-231. Really, we need legislation concerning the importation of exotic pets. If there is no agreement between any two countries in this regard, the net result is confusion and the destruction of birds or pets.
I suggest that it is not acceptable to bring in pets under the sorts of conditions I just outlined. In any event the climate of northern Canada is severe, and it takes exotic animals a couple of generations to adapt to our climate.
I wanted to tell the House those two stories which some may think humorous; actually the pigeons were the losers in the end. Of course the constituent who tried to bring them into Canada ended up by being a lot of money out of pocket, because bringing a parrot and six pigeons first-class from Yugoslavia to Winnipeg was somewhat expensive. He clearly did not understand that there was a law which prevented his bringing these birds to Canada. For all these reasons I support Bill C-231, Mr. Speaker.
